summary: It is an interactive educational PC simulation game.   It directly addresses the challenge by placing players in the role of an aerospace engineering team that must design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission from initial concept to orbital operations. Participants select target missions, orbits, scientific instruments, spacecraft subsystems, and launch rockets while balancing six interconnected capacity constraints—mass, electrical power, budget, data bandwidth, fuel, and manufacturing lead time—using a real-time traffic-light dashboard before facing dynamic in-flight hazards.   This project is important because it transforms abstract engineering and Capacity Planning principles into hands-on decision-making, teaching students and players how to evaluate trade-offs, identify system bottlenecks, manage safety margins, and collaborate across functional roles to achieve mission success.
details:
Proyecto Aurora: Space Mission Builder is an interactive educational PC simulation game where players step into the role of a multidisciplinary space mission engineering team guided by virtual mentor Captain Cosmo. Participants design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission from initial concept to orbital operations:

  1. Setup & Role Assignment: Players choose solo play, 2-to-4 player collaborative mode (with automatic departmental role rotation: Mission Chief, Scientist, Spacecraft Engineer, and Power & Communications Specialist), or multi-team tournament mode using a shared random event seed, alongside four difficulty levels (Easy, Normal, Expert, and Sandbox).
  2. Mission & Orbit Selection: Players select 1 of 5 space missions (Earth Observation, Lunar Water Search, Mars Climate Study, Solar Storm Monitoring, or Exoplanet Search) and an operational orbit (LEO, SSO, GEO, Lagrange L1/L2, Lunar, or Mars), each with unique lifespans, budgets, radiation levels, eclipse durations, and science multipliers.
  3. End-to-End Spacecraft Engineering: Players equip primary and secondary scientific instruments (11 sensor types) and configure subsystems—structural chassis, radiation shielding, onboard memory, attitude control, Chemical or Ion propulsion, propellant tanks, Solar panels or Nuclear RTG power, batteries, antennas, ground-station networks, and 1 of 4 launch rockets (Colibrí, Halcón, Quetzal, or Titán).
  4. Real-Time Traffic-Light Capacity Review: Before liftoff, a live dashboard evaluates six interconnected system constraints using a Green / Yellow / Red traffic-light indicator. Any Red alert (such as exceeding rocket payload capacity, budget, or launch window deadlines) blocks launch until the team negotiates engineering trade-offs.
  5. Flight Simulation & Diagnostic Report: During month-by-month orbital flight, players respond to random space hazards (Solar Storms, Space Debris, Martian Dust Storms, Micrometeorites, and hardware glitches). Afterward, an automated engine grades the mission on a 1,000-point scale, diagnoses root-cause bottlenecks, and compares the spacecraft against Captain Cosmo's algorithmic benchmark design.

Benefits of the Project

  • Visualizes Complex Systems & Bottlenecks: Translates abstract engineering and Capacity Planning principles—such as capacity utilization, bottlenecks (Theory of Constraints), safety cushions, and lead times—into immediate visual cause-and-effect feedback.
  • Systems Thinking & Trade-Off Analysis: Demonstrates that optimizing one variable (e.g., adding high-resolution telescopes) creates downstream pressure on mass, electrical power, data bandwidth, capital budget, and assembly lead time.
  • Cross-Functional Collaboration: Replicates real engineering departments, requiring players to negotiate resource allocation across specialized roles before committing to launch.
  • Zero-Friction Deployment: Packaged as a lightweight standalone Windows executable with built-in tutorials, an interactive technical glossary, and offline local leaderboard persistence.

Intended Impact

The project aims to bridge the gap between theoretical resource-management education and practical aerospace systems engineering. By allowing students and participants to experiment, fail safely, and iterate on complete space mission architectures in 10–15 minute sessions, Proyecto Aurora builds analytical decision-making skills, highlights the importance of preventive safety margins, and inspires interest in space mission design.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Programming Language: Python 3.
  • GUI & Custom Graphics: Python Tkinter library (used to build custom interactive dashboards, live visual spacecraft assembly previews, animated orbital trajectories, and real-time capacity gauges).
  • Data Persistence & Algorithms: Local JSON storage for persistent rankings/saved designs and custom heuristic optimization algorithms for Captain Cosmo's automated reference solver and root-cause diagnostic engine.
  • Hardware: Standard Windows 10/11 laptops and desktop PCs

How Is Our Project Creative?

Rather than relying on static quizzes or disconnected spreadsheets, Proyecto Aurora gamifies aerospace systems engineering through a cohesive narrative led by Captain Cosmo, dynamic orbital animations, and a multi-role negotiation mechanic. The custom traffic-light capacity engine turns six simultaneous physical and financial equations (rocket lift ratios,propulsion budgets, solar irradiance by distance, eclipse battery discharge, downlink data rates, and assembly lead times) into an intuitive, replayable strategy experience complete with competitive tournament seeds.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  1. Balancing Realism with Playability: Calibrating physics and engineering formulas so the simulation feels authentic to spaceflight without overwhelming non-specialist players.
  2. Interdependent Resource Coupling: Ensuring every component modification dynamically recalculates all six capacity constraints and departmental alerts in real time.
  3. Safety Margins vs. Over-Capacity Waste: Designing scoring and hazard mechanics that penalize both risky 99% capacity utilization (which fails during solar storms or eclipses) and wasteful over-sizing.
  4. Accessibility & Portability: Eliminating external dependencies and internet requirements so any classroom or evaluator on Windows can run the game immediately with a single click.
